name: Central African forest peoples
summary: The hunter-gatherers of the Central African rainforest, ancestors of today’s BaAka, Mbuti and other forest peoples. (The source maps label this area “Bantu” in early times, before Bantu-speaking farmers arrived.)

knownFor.label: Forest polyphonic singing
knownFor.note: Complex layered songs, recognised by UNESCO.

knownFor.label: Net hunting
knownFor.note: Groups drive animals into long nets.

knownFor.label: Honey gathering
knownFor.note: Climbing tall trees to collect wild honey.

location.value: Central Africa, mostly the Congo Basin.

terrain.value: Dense lowland rainforest of the Congo Basin, cut by rivers such as the Congo, Sangha and Ubangi, with swamps and patches of savanna.

climate.value: Hot, humid equatorial climate with rain in most months; drier phases, such as one around 3,000 years ago, opened gaps in the forest.

resources.value: Game such as duikers and monkeys, wild honey, nuts, fruits, wild yams, caterpillars and fish, and plants used for medicine and arrow poison.

disasters.value: No disasters are recorded; droughts in drier phases and river floods probably affected food supplies from time to time.

population.value: Unknown for early times; probably small, scattered bands of a few dozen people each.

urbanisation.value: No towns: people lived in small, temporary forest camps of a few huts, which moved several times a year with hunting and gathering.

disease.value: Malaria, yaws, intestinal parasites and other tropical diseases were probably common; in recent times outside contact brought new illnesses.

migration.value: The Bantu expansion began about 3,500 years ago (roughly 1500 BCE); earlier farming migrations began about 5,500 years ago.

economicBase.value: Mainly hunting and gathering: the Mbuti use nets, traps and bows, and gather yams, berries, fruits, roots, leaves and kola nuts. Bantu villagers trade iron goods, pots and basketry for meat, hides and other forest goods.

tradeRoutes.value: Forest goods such as meat, honey and wild plants were exchanged with neighbouring farmers for crops, iron tools, pots and salt.

wealth.value: Little private property; sharing was the rule.

moneyAndTax.value: No money and no taxes; goods were shared within the camp or bartered with farming villages.

inequality.value: Very equal: food, especially meat, was shared by custom, no one could give orders to others, and women had a strong say.

governmentType.value: No state: the page says Mbuti societies have no ruling group or lineage and little social structure; issues are discussed and decided by consensus at fire camps.

keyRulers.value: No rulers: the page describes no ruling group and never mentions chiefs.

succession.value: No office to inherit; camp members decided matters together, and people who disagreed could move to another camp.

institutions.value: Food-sharing rules, group net hunts, forest rituals such as the Mbuti molimo, and marriage ties linking different camps.

stability.value: Bands were flexible: when quarrels arose, families moved to another camp, which kept the wider way of life stable for thousands of years.

eliteConflict.value: No elites to compete; disputes were usually settled by joking, mockery or one side moving away.

armyAndTech.value: No armies; bows with poison-tipped arrows, spears and large hunting nets were used for hunting rather than war.

majorWars.value: The page describes no wars; it mentions only a later genocide campaign and civil unrest in the region.

territoryChange.value: Lost forest land to farmers and logging over time.

alliancesRivals.value: Long-term partnerships with farming villages, trading forest meat and honey for crops and iron; the relationship was often unequal.

inventions.value: Large communal hunting nets, poisoned arrows, ways of collecting wild honey, and knowledge of hundreds of food and medicinal plants.

scienceEducation.value: Deep knowledge of the forest, passed on orally.

openness.value: Open to neighbours: over time they adopted the languages of farming peoples and traded with them, while keeping a forest way of life.

communicationTransport.value: Travel on foot along forest paths and by canoe on rivers; news passed by word of mouth between camps.

religion.value: The forest is called 'mother' or 'father', seen as a sacred protector and provider, and the molimo festival is held to wake the forest after events such as the death of an important person.

languageWriting.value: They adopted the languages of neighbouring farmers (Bantu, Ubangian and Central Sudanic); Aka and Baka keep non-Bantu, non-Ubangian vocabulary, about 30% of the lexicon.

artsArchitecture.value: Dense, contrapuntal vocal polyphony (found among the Aka–Baka and Mbuti, not the Gyele or Twa); the n’dehou bamboo flute.

socialStructure.value: Small, equal bands of related families with no ranks; age and skill earned respect, and men and women both took part in decisions.

sharedIdentity.value: A strong identity as people of the forest, distinct from farming villagers, kept alive through music, ritual and hunting.

dailyLife.value: Dome-shaped huts of branches and leaves; game, honey, nuts and tubers.

neighbours.value: Bantu-speaking farmers from roughly 1500 BCE onward, as well as Ubangian and Central Sudanic-speaking farmers in the north and east.

ideasReligions.value: Ideas of the forest as the source of life and goodness; in recent centuries some groups also took up Christianity or farmers’ beliefs.

colonisation.value: Later affected by colonial logging and conservation areas.

riseSignals.value: Long adaptation to the rainforest; genetic studies suggest their ancestors split from other African populations more than 60,000 years ago.

peakPeriod.value: No single peak; the forest way of life was probably most widespread before farmers moved into the forest from about 1500 BCE.

declineSignals.value: Loss of forest land to farming, logging and conservation parks, together with discrimination and pressure to settle in villages.

outcome.value: About 900,000 Pygmies were estimated in the central African forests in 2016, about 60% in the DRC.

overallCertainty.value: Mostly known from genetics, linguistics and ethnography.
